item.title: [Retailing 101 #9] Every Aisle Is a Small Business, and It Has Its Own P&L
item.body:
> One-line summary: Advanced merchandising means running each category like a standalone business — giving it a job to do, measuring the return on the cash parked in its inventory, and setting prices that protect both margin and price image.

## Today's Concept

Last time we met the person who picked everything on the shelf six months before you walked in. Today: how they actually decide. Three levers do most of the work.

**1. Category management — the aisle has a job.**
Instead of buying product by product, retailers group items the way shoppers think about them ("oral care," not "tubes we get from Colgate") and manage that group as a business unit. The framework, popularized in the 1990s through the industry's Efficient Consumer Response push, starts by assigning each category a **role**:

- **Destination** — a reason to choose this store over the one down the road. Deep assortment, sharp prices, lots of space.
- **Routine** — the everyday workhorse that builds the basket and carries margin. Most of the store lives here.
- **Occasional / seasonal** — grilling supplies in June, school glue in August.
- **Convenience** — you didn't come for it, but it's there. Fewer options, healthier margins.

The role drives everything downstream: how many SKUs, how much shelf, how aggressive the price, how much promo money. A destination category and a convenience category get opposite treatment on purpose.

One wrinkle worth knowing: retailers often name a **category captain** — usually the biggest supplier — to help build the plan, since that vendor has the best data. It's efficient and it's a conflict of interest at the same time, which is why captains' recommendations get audited and why the practice draws antitrust attention.

**2. Inventory management — the shelf is a bank account.**
Every unit on that shelf is cash the retailer can't use for anything else. So the question isn't "did it sell?" but "what did it earn per dollar tied up?" Two numbers carry the load:

```
inventory turnover = cost of goods sold / average inventory at cost
GMROI = gross margin dollars / average inventory at cost
weeks of supply = 52 / annual turns
```

GMROI of 2.5 means the category returned $2.50 of gross margin for every $1 invested in inventory. This is why a low-margin item that turns 20 times a year can beat a high-margin item that turns twice — and why buyers argue about turns more than about markup.

The counterweight is service level. Order less and you free cash but risk an out-of-stock, which costs the sale and sometimes the trip. So teams hold **safety stock** and set a reorder point:

```
reorder point = expected demand during lead time + safety stock
```

Then there's leakage. **Shrink** — theft, damage, spoilage, paperwork errors — has run around 1.5% of sales in recent National Retail Federation security surveys. On thin retail margins, that's not rounding.

**3. Pricing — margin and image, at the same time.**
The arithmetic is easy:

```
retail price = cost / (1 - target margin %)
```

"Keystone" markup just means doubling cost: a $5 item retails at $10, a 50% margin. The strategy is the hard part, and it splits two ways. **EDLP** (everyday low price) keeps prices flat and predictable — Walmart, Costco, Aldi. **High–low** runs a base price plus frequent, deep promotions, often gated behind a loyalty card — most conventional supermarkets and department stores. EDLP smooths demand and cuts labor spent re-ticketing; high–low creates urgency and pulls in deal-sensitive shoppers, at the cost of training people to wait for the sale.

Either way, no one prices 40,000 items with equal care. Shoppers only remember a few dozen **key value items** — milk, eggs, bananas, a 12-pack of soda — and those set the store's price image. Those get priced sharply, sometimes at or below cost as a **loss leader**, and the margin is recovered on the rest of the basket. (Loss leaders are generally legal, though a number of states have minimum-markup laws, usually covering gas, alcohol, or tobacco.) And when inventory ages, **markdowns** are the release valve: a planned cadence of cuts that converts stale stock back into cash before it's worth nothing.

## In Everyday Life

Sunday morning, a Kroger on the north side of Columbus. Your cart: a gallon of milk, cereal, toothpaste, tortilla chips, a rotisserie chicken.

The milk is a key value item. It's priced within pennies of the Meijer two miles away because management assumes you know roughly what milk costs. The rotisserie chicken is close to a loss leader — cooked from a bird that would've been marked down anyway, priced to get you through the door on the one trip where you might also buy a $30 cut of steak. Costco has famously held its chicken at $4.99 for years for exactly this reason.

The toothpaste tells the category story. Oral care is a routine category here, so you get maybe 40 SKUs, not 90, and the shelf runs a familiar pattern: a national brand at eye level, the Kroger store brand right beside it at a lower price and a higher margin, and the $9 whitening kit on the top shelf where it turns slowly but earns well when it does. The chips are near the front — high turns, decent margin, impulse-friendly placement.

And the endcap you walked past with the seasonal cooler display? That's an occasional category, bought in a single seasonal buy, with a markdown schedule already written for late August. Nobody will scramble when it stops selling. That was the plan in April.

## Three-Line Recap

1. Category management treats each group of products as a business with an assigned role — destination, routine, occasional, or convenience — and that role drives assortment, space, and price aggressiveness.
2. Inventory is capital, so retailers judge it by turns and GMROI (gross margin per dollar invested), balancing that against the cost of being out of stock.
3. Pricing is a portfolio: sharp on the handful of key value items that shape price image, and recovered across everything else — under either an EDLP or a high–low strategy.

## ✅ Self Quiz

**1.** A category posts a GMROI of 3.0. What does that mean?
  A) It sold three times more than last year
  B) It earned $3.00 of gross margin per $1 invested in inventory at cost
  C) Its gross margin is 30%
  D) It turns three times per week

**2.** O / X — An EDLP retailer's core strategy is running deep weekly promotions to create urgency.

**3.** In a supermarket, "milk and eggs, priced to match the competitor down the street" is best described as:
  A) A convenience category
  B) A seasonal buy
  C) Key value items in a destination/traffic-driving role
  D) A markdown cadence

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Category management** — Managing a group of related products as a single business unit with its own role, strategy, and scorecard, rather than item by item.
- **Category role** — The job assigned to a category (destination, routine, occasional/seasonal, convenience), which determines its space, assortment breadth, and pricing posture.
- **GMROI** — Gross margin return on inventory investment: gross margin dollars divided by average inventory at cost; the profit earned per dollar tied up in stock.
- **Inventory turnover** — How many times a year inventory is sold and replaced (COGS ÷ average inventory at cost); higher turns free up cash and reduce markdown risk.
- **EDLP vs. high–low** — Two pricing strategies: consistently low everyday prices, versus a higher base price punctuated by frequent deep promotions.

---

*Answers: 1 — B. GMROI is gross margin dollars ÷ average inventory at cost, so 3.0 means $3.00 of gross margin per $1 of inventory investment. It says nothing directly about margin percentage or growth. 2 — X (False). That describes high–low pricing; EDLP deliberately avoids the promo cycle in favor of stable, predictable prices. 3 — C. Milk and eggs are classic key value items whose prices shoppers actually remember, so they're priced to build traffic and price image, with margin recovered elsewhere in the basket.*
